extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, astronomers, navigators, and experimental scientists (17th-century observers and experimenters)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and recommended observational/experimental practices for lunar eclipses, compass variation, sounding, tidal and wind measurements, pneumatic experiments, and natural-history observations as presented in a 17th-century Philosophical Transactions volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of telescope for geographical lunar-eclipse observations
rubrics_metrics.description: For geographical purposes a telescope is practicable and necessary; naked-eye times differ considerably from telescopic ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because naked-eye times differ from telescopic observations, because true shadow and penumbra are hard to distinguish without prior practice, and because beginnings/ends are often unfit for precise observation (slow change due to oblique motion of the shadow), use a telescope and prior familiarization with the line separating shadow and penumbra before principal observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select and use fixed lunar surface spots for eclipse timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a select number of the most eminent spots on the moon's surface to be constantly used in all parts of the world (examples: Mons Sinai, Etna, Porphyrites, Scrorum, Insula Besbicus, Creta, Palus Mseotis, Mareeotis, Lacus Niger Major).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In each eclipse observe (for instance) three of these spots near the ecliptic: note when they are first touched by the true shadow, when they are just completely entered into it, and in the decrease when they are first fully clear from the true shadow. These spot-based contacts are less susceptible to penumbral ambiguity and slow appearance changes than timings of beginning/end of totality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record altitudes of fixed stars at eclipse contact moments
rubrics_metrics.description: At the accurate determinations of contact moments take altitudes of remarkable fixed stars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take altitudes of stars chosen with regard to their position relative to the meridian: those between the equator and tropic of Cancer on this side of the line, those beyond the line situated toward the other tropic, and in all places choose stars that at the time of observation are about four hours distant from the meridian. Use these star altitudes to fix the time/meridian reference for geographical determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using beginning/end of eclipse or total darkness as primary geodetic markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Times of beginning, middle, and end of eclipses, especially beginning/end of total darkness, are often not reliable for geographical determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: naked-eye vs telescope discrepancy; indistinctness between true shadow and penumbra even with glasses unless observer has previously seen the separating line; small partial eclipses and short totalities change appearances slowly due to oblique shadow motion. Prefer spot-contact timings with telescopic observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and record compass variation at land and sea
rubrics_metrics.description: To observe the variation of the compass/needle: at land use fixed dials and instruments to find the meridian; at sea employ ring-dials set to exact hour or compare sun's true azimuth with the needle's magnetic azimuth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At sea find the sun's true azimuth by knowing pole height, sun's declination, and altitude and constructing a spherical oblique-angled triangle of the three complements; compute angle at zenith and subtract from 180 to get sun's true azimuth. Subtract magnetical azimuth (needle) from true azimuth to obtain variation; if magnetic azimuth is less, variation is on same side as sun, if greater, on the other. Also possible to use stars by finding true north/meridian. Do both sun and stars for greater certainty; with careful work variation can be found to degrees, half-degrees, and even minutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dipping needle to measure magnetic dip
rubrics_metrics.description: When examining the dipping needle, hang its circle perpendicular and turn it until it is in the magnetical meridian where it dips most; note the degree of its depression under the horizon and record in a table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the dipping needle at least as often as the compass-variation experiment; the circle should be hung perpendicular and adjusted to the magnetic meridian for maximum dip measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record tidal particulars comprehensively
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief particulars of the tides to be recorded are the precise times of the beginnings of the flood and ebb, direction and timing of currents, perpendicular heights and depths of the tide, lowest ebb, and relations to moon age and time of year for highest/lowest tides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note how currents run in all places, their times and changes; record which day of the moon's age and what times of year highest and lowest tides occur. Precise timing is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound depth without a line using a timed floating-globe-and-weight apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a varnished wooden globe with a springing wire and detachable weight; sink it to the bottom so the weight stops first and the globe continues to move allowing the spring to release and the globe to reascend; observe time under water and use tables to compute depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instrument details: globe of fir or maple well secured from imbibing water; weight heavier than globe; long wire staple and springing wire with bended end that holds weight until stopped by bottom. Time the globe's stay with a watch (minutes/seconds), minute-glass, or pendulum vibrating seconds; calibrate with trials (examples from Thames: 19 ft => 6 seconds; 10 ft => 3.5 seconds). Repeat trials, document ball and lead weights and geometry, and account for currents and instrument adjustments (conical leads, iron crooks) to ensure reliable contact and release at the bottom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document trials and calibrations when using new sounding instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: When trialing the sounding-without-line instrument, record weights and dimensions of balls and leads, number of pendulum vibrations or time intervals, and repeat trials to confirm consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: record weights (oz./gr.), depths (fathoms), number of pendulum strokes; repeat trials at same depth to check reproducibility; note when ball fails to reach bottom (very short return times) and adjust lead shape/crook to carry ball down and release reliably. Account for boat drift and subsurface currents that may carry the rising ball laterally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure wind force with a deflecting-flat instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure strength of winds by exposing an instrument with a flat side to the wind; the degrees to which the flat side is raised indicate force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set the flat side right against the wind; the number of degrees on the limb to which the wind raises that flat side shows the wind's force in proportion to the resistance of the instrument's flat side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine salt-water specific gravity by narrow-neck phial and salt residue
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a very narrow-neck glass phial: fill drop by drop until it holds no more, dry the phial and weigh; then evaporate the water and weigh dry salt to determine proportion of salt by weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the empty phial first. When filling, add water drop by drop until full, drying and then weighing to get sample mass. Evaporate gently to dryness to leave salt, weigh the residue to compute proportion of salt to sample weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve sea-compass quality via needle touching, balancing, and variation calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfection of sea compasses depends on needles being touched by good load-stones, being well balanced, and having the variation truly placed; propose showing variation to minutes and seconds for greater perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested inquiries/experiments: (1) Whether a needle can be so touched on any magnet as not to point to true north/south (test in places of unknown variation); (2) Whether different load-stones give different directions; (3) Whether fainter or stronger touches on same magnet cause variation in direction. For these tests procure as many load-stones and a good number of exactly made needles of the same metal, size, and figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pneumatic-engine (air-pump) experiments on plants, seeds, grafts, and eggs
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose experiments to see effects of exhausting air on plants (with earth about roots), seeds (germination), sensitive plants, grafted pears, and silkworm eggs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested trials: (1) Put flourishing plants (with earth around roots) into an exhausted receiver to see if they suddenly wither; (2) Try whether seeds (fast-growing: orpin, lettuce, garden cress) will germinate and thrive in exhausted receiver; (3) Whether exclusion of air harms sensitive plants; (4) Whether grafting pears upon spina cervina communicates purging quality to fruit; (5) Whether silkworm eggs will hatch in exhausted receiver during hatching season. Report prior experiment: lettuce seed in exhausted receiver did not germinate while control in open air grew; readmission of air allowed subsequent germination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural-history observational protocol for ants (microscopy and behavioral recording)
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying ants: classify sorts (black, dark brown, feuillemort), note distinct habitations, record interspecific interactions, open banks to observe 'white substance' (eggs), use microscope to examine developmental stages from spawn to maggot to chrysalid to ant, and record care-for-young behaviors and diurnal placement patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open banks to find white soft substance resembling fine sugar; under microscope open and examine membranes and stages; observe maggot motion, transformation timing (film covering maggot while transforming), black speck near anus and its disappearance, and that ants carry away and reassemble their spawn when disturbed. Note time-of-day patterns: young are brought toward the top in summer mornings, and toward deeper levels when weather cools; test deception with scattered food—ants will not touch non-offspring material even if humans are fooled.
